extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychoanalysis, literary theory, and humor studies (undergraduate/graduate seminar audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing and analyzing Freud's categories, techniques, social conditions, and psychoanalytic account of jokes, the comic, and humor from Jokes (Witz) and their Relation to the Unconscious (1905). Intended as an academic précis for classroom discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witz (the Joke) — three-person structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Witz requires three persons: one in cooperation with the teller laughing at a third’s expense; it is Janus-faced and takes advantage of ambiguity in a wit that can be used against another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud sees this arising from 'an economy of expenditure in inhibition.' The social role of a third (often a target) is central; jokes function as a cooperative act aimed at another and rely on social dynamics of attack/masking.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Comic — two-person comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comic requires two persons because, as 'an economy of expenditure in thought,' it compares and contrasts another with a certain standard or action; this includes physical caricature or buffoonery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comic is mimetic and based on bodily and psychical imitation; it privileges comparison/contrast and often involves physical exaggeration or caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor — solitary sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor needs only one person since, as 'an economy of expenditure of feeling,' one has sympathy with the teller (even if the teller is oneself).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor can be mixed with joke or comic forms and can coexist with painful emotions; it does not require an external target in the same way Witz does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form as a requirement for the amusing
rubrics_metrics.description: The amusing requires form: the form of the joke (witz, comic scenario, humorous story) takes up the bulk of analysis and generally involves conciseness of word choice and delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form often uses substitution of words/concepts, the absurd, or physical elements; tight integration of form and content is critical for the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and social context shape jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Content and context, examined with reference to social tendencies of display and aggression, shape the joke in a variety of ways and influence hearers' responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social tendencies (class, gender, authority relations) determine allowable targets and whether certain wit will function as control, aggression, or release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconscious energies and economy of psychic expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: For Freud, the amusing also requires the unconscious energies of his broader theories — jokes gratify prohibited tendencies through an 'economy of psychic expenditure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor/Witz can act as comic catharsis: a free discharge of latent energies that ties psychic economy to social expression and pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbal and ideational condensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of mixed word-formation and modification (whole/part; change of order; slight modification; full sense) as a technique of joke construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condensation compresses ideas/words to produce surprise or double sense; often operates at the level of morphological or syntactic change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double meaning (puns, ambiguity, allusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploitation of proper name significance, metaphorical versus verbal meaning, play on words, ambiguity, and allusion to generate wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-meaning devices rely on listener recognition of alternate senses; names, metaphors, and cultural allusions are common loci for this technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other verbal/ideational changes (puns, double-wit, omission, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: A variety of devices including puns, double-wit in which is removed, nonsense, automatic error, unification, representation by opposition, outdoing-wit, indirect allusion, omission, least-wit, direct comparison, forced or particular attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud catalogs many specific maneuvers; these techniques manipulate expectations, produce misreadings, or use deliberate insufficiency to provoke laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and Pleasure of the Naïve (comic subtype)
rubrics_metrics.description: We laugh at the person who naively stumbles on the comic, especially when their innocence is expected (e.g., children).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The naive's lack of awareness produces a pleasure in witnessing unintentional comic revelation; Freud links this to infantile sources of comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion-Based Comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy arising from physically funny action: we sympathetically feel and evaluate the action, often judging it excessive or deficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Has a basis in ideational mimicry; physicality and timing are crucial, and the spectator often identifies bodily expectations that are subverted or exaggerated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situation-Based Comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy arising from more complex routines and situations rather than single motions; may provoke feelings of superiority over the characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situation-based forms often involve routines, repeated motifs, or social contexts that produce comic contrast or misunderstanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation-Based Comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy derived from our ability to anticipate future outcomes; bodily identification with potential outcomes of motions or actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pleasure stems from anticipation and violation or confirmation of expectations; Freud suggests this is reducible to mimicry tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation-Based Comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure of imitating another; comic often involves superior/inferior contrast and the degrading or spoofing of an inadequate target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes parody, travesty, and intentional inadequacy asSpoofing devices; imitation is central to many comic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Being disposed towards laughter (one of six maximizing characteristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disposition or readiness to laugh increases the chance that something will register as comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience mood and predisposition are critical contextual factors in whether comic stimuli succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of comic pleasure (maximizing characteristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The expectation that something will be comic predisposes one to find it funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing and prior cues can prime an audience to receive material as humorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: No cognitive distractions (maximizing characteristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Absence of cognitive distractions is necessary to allow laughter to occur unimpeded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If listeners are mentally occupied, the comic stimulus may fail; attention and cognitive bandwidth matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not focused on correcting the behavior (maximizing characteristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic pleasure is maximized when the response is not oriented toward correcting the behavior at hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the social impulse is to fix or shame rather than enjoy, laughter is inhibited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to be objective towards the behavior (maximizing characteristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ability to adopt an objective stance about the behavior increases comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional detachment permits amusement; intense personal involvement can block comic reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility of associated pleasures (maximizing characteristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Associated pleasures (e.g., sensual or social pleasures) must be compatible to support comic enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflicting concurrent pleasures or disgust can reduce comedic response; harmony of pleasures aids laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmless wit (psychological tendency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Harmless wit intends mutual enjoyment for all who hear and functions as a kind of control group in Freud's taxonomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designed to produce shared amusement without aggression or transgression; socially affiliative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual wit, obscenity, exhibitionism
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms that use smut or cloaked sexual jokes to release sexual desire for another present or to involve others in desire for the absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can appear as attempted seduction or masked aggression; often taps into repressed sexual impulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hostile wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit used as a socially acceptable way to attack another (e.g., class- or gender-based invective); rebellion against authority masked through rejoinder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions as displaced aggression; target choice and social norms determine whether hostility is permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cynical, skeptical, and blasphemous wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Types of wit allowing expression of negatively judged attitudes more safely, including self-criticism by a despised group in milder form than criticism by a powerful party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permits taboo sentiments to be voiced under the cover of humor; social position of speaker matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the third person and surprise in social shaping of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: The third person functions as comic judge or evaluator and surprise for that third party in the humorous contrast is important for the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social reactions, the presence of a judge/audience, and their surprise are key to Witz as a social act; questions about judge and target overlapping (e.g., gallows humor) are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure in ideational and verbal formation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is pleasure in ideational and verbal formation of jokes — in discovery of the unfamiliar and recovery of the familiar that goes unnoticed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cognitive delight in sudden perception or insight contributes to humor; recognition is pleasurable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure in returning to childhood behaviors, play, and jest
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes allow a return to childish play and behaviors, yielding a form of pleasure tied to infancy and playfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regression and play-pleasure are psychoanalytic sources of humor enjoyment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure in overcoming shame
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes permit a general overcoming of shame by allowing prohibited tendencies to be expressed socially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor can function to remove inhibitions and provide relief from shame through social expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fore-pleasure: combining play-pleasure with removal-pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Witz has a quality of fore-pleasure that brings together play-pleasure with removal-pleasure, assisting the teller to express normally unacceptable material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This psychoanalytic concept links anticipatory pleasure with the social act of discharging inhibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit-work as foreconscious elaboration captured by consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: A foreconscious thought is left to unconscious elaboration and the results are then grasped by conscious perception (wit-work phenomenon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wit often emerges quickly from preconscious processes and is recognized immediately, giving a sense of suddenness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity and conciseness of wit (rapid, unplanned emergence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The brevity and conciseness of wit often appears quickly without time for planning and is elaborated only in retrospect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economy of expression and timing are essential technical virtues of successful witticisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regression to infancy and basic desires in wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit involves regressions to infantile states and basic desires; these regressions underlie play and sexual elements of jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychoanalytic reading highlights how jokes tap early psychic structures and impulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit-work is more limited than dream-work
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit-work does not have the same complete freedom as dream-work; use of the opposite or absurdity is more limited by technique in jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical constraints of social intelligibility and form limit how far jokes can employ dream-like transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witz as a social (not purely individual) activity
rubrics_metrics.description: While dreams are about the individual alone, Witz is a social activity; the individual pleasure is only one aspect of its function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes must be understood as acts embedded in social relations — teller, audience, and target dynamics are integral.
